source: Downes (1990) Herbert Simon's Computational Models of Scientific Discovery (PSA 1990 vol 1)
finding: Core critique of the case-study-to-program method (BACON, KEKADA). Lab notebooks are not think-aloud protocols, so heuristics read out of them are inferred, not observed.
numbers: Krebs case: the assistant Henseleit did much of the experimental work and note-taking, yet KEKADA models one solitary mind.
limits: A critic, not a replication. Rival view: discovery is partly social (acceptance, Brannigan 1981). Downes does not run KEKADA on new data.
agent_relevance: Operator sequences mined from case histories are hypotheses about process, not records. Treat them as candidate operators and test them (G7).

source: Downes (1990) on the sufficiency claim for BACON and KEKADA
finding: BACON-style programs rediscover Kepler's third law (D^3/P^2 = c), Boyle and Snell with rules like 'if two terms increase together, consider their ratio'. Simon claims only sufficiency of the mechanisms.
numbers: Programs: BACON family, KEKADA (Krebs, ornithine cycle). No test of necessity.
quote: finding a set of mechanisms that is sufficient to account for discovery
limits: Reproducing a known result may use a path unlike the historical one. Data were chosen by the programmers.
agent_relevance: A suite of operators that reproduces a known result shows it can suffice, not that it generalizes. Hold-out discoveries are needed.

source: Downes (1990): reasons versus process in notebooks and papers
finding: Published papers give plausible reasons after the fact (cf. Nisbett and Wilson 1977). No principled method separates real process from tidy reconstruction.
numbers: Example: Millikan's notebooks hold columns of figures and notes such as 'beautiful, publish this', not records of thought.
limits: Argument from the verbal-report literature, not a measured effect.
agent_relevance: Case studies are rationalized. Prefer sources that log the order of actions (diaries, code histories) over later accounts.

source: Tweney, Anderson, Cavicchi et al. (2003) Representational, Textual, and Experimental Practices: The Case of Michael Faraday (CogSci 25)
finding: Cognitive-historical work on Faraday uses diaries plus physical replication. Over 600 surviving specimens from Faraday's 1856 gold research were keyed to diary entries.
numbers: More than 600 specimens; replication of some specimens used to re-trace how confusion became lawful relations.
limits: Symposium abstract, no effect sizes. Replication here means re-doing the experiments, not statistical replication.
agent_relevance: Re-running the logged procedure is a stronger check on a case story than reading the diary alone.

source: Tweney and Ayala (2003) Artifacts of Memory: Michael Faraday and the Construction of Meaning (CogSci 25)
finding: Faraday's diary has 16,041 numbered entries (1832-1860). He built retrieval slips and sheets (at least 12 sheet types) to reorder entries and to draft papers. The notebook was an active tool.
numbers: 16041 entries; at least 12 retrieval-sheet types; hundreds of slips and sheets survive; watermark dates tie sheets to the diary paper.
limits: Content analysis and physical dating, no control cases. One scientist.
agent_relevance: Candidate operator: re-index one's own trial log to find patterns. Maps to logged attempts reorganised by code (G2).

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: Standard rediscovery test built from the Feynman Lectures. AI Feynman solved all 100 basic equations; the commercial Eureqa solved 71%.
numbers: 100 basic equations: AI Feynman 100%, Eureqa 71%. 20 bonus equations: AI Feynman 90%, Eureqa 15%. Eureqa ran on 4 CPUs per equation.
limits: Textbook equations, clean data. Later work shows LLMs have memorized these same equations.
agent_relevance: A pass on Feynman is not discovery evidence for an LLM agent because of contamination.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs, appendix C
finding: Memorization check: LLM-SR with GPT-3.5 reaches low NMSE on Feynman problems within a few iterations, often in one pass. Mixtral perplexity is far lower on Feynman equations than on new problems.
numbers: Example perplexities: Feynman items about 1.94 to 2.04; a new-benchmark item 6.24. Low NMSE in fewer than 20 iterations on Feynman.
limits: Perplexity is a proxy, not proof. One backbone (Mixtral) for perplexity, GPT-3.5 for the curves.
agent_relevance: Famous-law rediscovery by an LLM is largely recall. Use novel or counterfactual variants to measure operators (G8).

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: scientific equation discovery with LLMs (ICML 2025)
finding: 239 problems (111 LSR-Transform, 128 LSR-Synth) built to defeat memorization. The best system reaches only 31.5% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform and 28.1% on LSR-Synth.
numbers: Table 1, LSR-Transform symbolic accuracy: LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini 31.53%, Llama-3.1-8B 30.63%, GPT-3.5-turbo 10.81%. Direct prompting without data: GPT-4o-mini 7.21%.
limits: Symbolic accuracy judged by GPT-4o (94.6% agreement with humans on a sample). Three LLMs only.
agent_relevance: Even with data feedback and evolutionary search, recovering the true form is under one third once the form is not memorized.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: data-driven methods versus direct prompting
finding: Methods with data feedback beat prompting without data. LSR-Transform Acc0.1: LaSR 45.94 to 50.45%, LLM-SR 10.81 to 39.64%, direct prompting 1.8 to 13.9%.
numbers: LaSR GPT-4o-mini 50.45% but only 6.31% symbolic accuracy; LLM-SR GPT-4o-mini 39.64% Acc0.1 and 31.53% symbolic.
limits: Method ranking flips between symbolic and numeric metrics. Some SGA cells were unreadable in the extracted text and are not quoted.
agent_relevance: A good numeric fit and the right form are different things. Supports G3: check on held-out data and on structure.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: textbook form versus transformed form
finding: The same physical problems written in a transformed mathematical form give lower accuracy than the textbook form at equal complexity. Fig. 1 shows sharp error rises on the new data.
numbers: Figure 4 reports the gap in symbolic accuracy and Acc0.1 averaged over all method-LLM pairs. Exact gap not available in extracted text.
limits: Direction stated clearly; magnitude not extracted.
agent_relevance: A controlled test that separates recall from reasoning. Apparent skill falls when surface form changes.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: benchmarking generalizable scientific law discovery in LLM agents (ICLR 2026)
finding: 324 tasks over 12 physics domains with counterfactual law shifts, probed interactively. Frontier models show a fragile ability: GPT-5 75.9% and Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4% overall; several other models below 10%.
numbers: 108 shifted laws x 3 model systems (Vanilla Equation, Simple System, Complex System), 11 LLMs. Hardest setting: GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all other reasoning models below 6%.
limits: Simulated laws. Symbolic accuracy judged by an LLM (98.3% agreement with human experts reported).
agent_relevance: Interactive probing with counterfactual laws is the right test of operator sequences. System complexity is the main failure driver.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: noise and code-tool effects
finding: Noise of only 0.0001 cuts symbolic accuracy by 12 to 16% from the noise-free case; accuracy keeps falling to noise 0.1. A code interpreter helps weaker models (SA below 40%) but slightly hurts stronger ones.
numbers: Four noise levels: 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1. Code did not change noise robustness.
limits: The mechanism (early shift from exploring to exploiting) is the authors' reading of traces, not an intervention test.
agent_relevance: Tool access can cause premature closure. Let a signal, not tool availability, end exploration (G1).

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: towards data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: 264 real tasks derived from published papers in 6 domains plus 903 synthetic tasks. The best system scores only 25%.
numbers: Best non-oracle performance peaks at 25%. By domain, economics 25% and sociology 23% do better.
limits: Gold hypotheses come from papers likely in training data. LLM judge matches hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Success depends on the workflow type. Choose the operator by sub-task.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: a virtual environment for developing and evaluating automated scientific discovery agents
finding: 120 tasks, 8 topics, 3 difficulty levels. 11 practicing scientists completed 66% of tasks on average (knowledge score 55%). The best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks.
numbers: Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge tasks. Humans exceeded 60% completion on 11 of 16 tasks.
limits: Human sample is 11 people on one seed. Unit-test tasks were about 60%+ for agents, so components work, end-to-end fails.
agent_relevance: Humans sometimes brute-forced without explaining, so score completion and understanding apart.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: LLMs for rediscovering unseen chemistry scientific hypotheses (ICLR 2025)
finding: Contamination-controlled rediscovery: 51 chemistry papers published after January 2024, tested with an LLM trained before 2024. Retrieval of the true inspiration papers is high: GPT-4o 96.7% (top 20%), 83.7% (top 4%), 60.8% (top 0.8%).
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B 71.6 / 43.5 / 26.8%; Llama-3.1-70B 95.1 / 83.0 / 59.5%; Llama-3.1-405B 95.7 / 78.7 / 52.7%. Corpus of 300; hit ratio averaged over 51 papers.
limits: Backgrounds and inspirations were annotated by chemists after the fact. Hypotheses judged by two chemistry PhD students.
agent_relevance: Case-style decomposition (background, distant source, combination) is a usable operator sequence. Small models lose a lot at tight retrieval.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: the three-step decomposition
finding: The paper argues that retrieving inspirations, composing hypotheses and ranking them is a sufficient set of subtasks. More than 75% of true inspirations were covered by only the top 4% of the corpus.
numbers: Same 51-paper benchmark; top 4% selection by screening windows of 15 papers keeping 3.
quote: the most advanced LLMs might already know lots of knowledge pairs
limits: Authors call this a bold assumption. Sufficiency is argued, not proved.
agent_relevance: Matches problem-solving views of discovery: search for analogical sources then recombine.

source: Liu et al. (2026) ResearchBench: benchmarking LLMs in scientific discovery via inspiration-based task decomposition
finding: Large benchmark over 12 disciplines splitting discovery into inspiration retrieval, hypothesis composition and ranking. The authors report surprisingly high retrieval accuracy.
numbers: Exact numbers not recorded: only the abstract, introduction and retrieval paragraph were read.
limits: Extraction of paper components is done by an LLM, checked by experts. Closer papers are more likely to be picked, a bias.
agent_relevance: Retrieval seems easier than composition and ranking. Spend compute on composition and code-checked selection.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review found AI ideas more novel than human expert ideas (p < 0.05), but not better on feasibility. Mean novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition; 79 reviewers; 298 reviews; 49 idea writers from 26 institutions. Reviewer agreement only 56.1% on top vs bottom 25%.
limits: Ideas were not executed. Topic area was NLP prompting. Novelty judged by people with low agreement.
agent_relevance: Opinion-based novelty is noisy; consistent with G8.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024): diversity collapse and LLM judges
finding: More generation gives repeats: of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 were non-duplicates (similarity cutoff 0.8). LLM judges are poor evaluators of ideas.
numbers: GPT-4o direct ranking 50.0% balanced accuracy against human reviewer consistency 56.1%.
limits: Similarity cutoff is a design choice. Other judge configurations in the same table scored higher; only the GPT-4o direct figure is quoted.
agent_relevance: Scaling idea count has a ceiling; do not let an LLM pick the winner (G5, G8).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Hypothesis generation with large language models (HypoGeniC)
finding: Iterative hypothesis generation with a bandit-style reward improves accuracy over few-shot prompting by 31.7% on a synthetic dataset and by 13.9%, 3.3% and 24.9% on three real datasets.
numbers: Also beats supervised learning by 12.1% and 11.6% on two datasets.
limits: Classification-style hypotheses on labeled examples, not law discovery. Training accuracy is the reward and may overfit.
agent_relevance: Training score as reward, held-out score as the final test, fits G3 and G5.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: Full pipeline makes papers at under $15 each. The automated reviewer gets F1 0.57 vs 0.49 and AUC 0.65 for both against humans, but accuracy is below the 73% human figure from NeurIPS 2021.
numbers: Generated papers show hallucinated results tables, invented facts such as hardware, and invalid file paths.
limits: Small experiment templates. The reviewer is an LLM and can favour LLM text.
agent_relevance: Hallucinated experiments show why every revision must cite real code output (G2).

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench: toward rigorous assessment of language agents for data-driven scientific discovery (ICLR 2025)
finding: 102 tasks from 44 papers in four disciplines. The best agent solved 32.4% alone and 34.3% with expert knowledge; o1-preview reached 42.2% at more than 10 times the cost.
numbers: Three attempts per task; five LLMs and three frameworks (direct prompting, OpenHands CodeAct, self-debug).
limits: Tasks are programs for known analyses, not discovery from scratch.
agent_relevance: More inference compute helps but costs a lot; fits G7.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
finding: Multi-agent system (generation, reflection, ranking, evolution, proximity, meta-review). In one case it independently proposed the cf-PICI mechanism that a lab had found but not yet published.
numbers: Elo of top hypotheses rose with compute over 203 research goals; no saturation seen. AML drug candidates lab-tested; IC50 as low as 2 nM in three of four AML lines.
limits: Elo is auto-evaluated by the system's own ranking agents. The rediscovery is one instance reported by the authors.
agent_relevance: Self-rated gains from generate-debate-evolve loops need external validation. Count only what a check confirms.

source: Li et al. (2025) AI-Newton: concept-driven physical law discovery without prior knowledge
finding: On 46 classical mechanics experiments the system rediscovered Newton's second law, energy conservation and universal gravitation from raw data with no prior physics.
numbers: Runs average 48 hours with up to 1200 trials; about 90 concepts and 50 general laws per run on average.
limits: Simulated experiments; concepts proposed in a hand-built domain language.
agent_relevance: Laws are built stepwise: propose a concept, then generalize. Progressive generalization is a candidate operator.

source: Tweney et al. (2003) CogSci symposium: list of cognitive-historical methods
finding: The symposium lists the main cognitive-historical works: Gooding 1990, Gorman 1997, Klahr and Simon 1999, Nersessian 1999, Tweney 2001. All lean on a few richly documented cases, such as Faraday.
numbers: Faraday's diary and notebook record is very large and partly published (Martin 1931-36).
limits: I read only this citation list, not the cited works.
agent_relevance: The field rests on a few rich cases; generalizing to other fields is untested.
